title: The Doctor China Remembered
shortDescription: A doctor from a middle-class family in Solapur who sailed to China in 1938 with a five-man medical mission, operated for the Communist Eighth Route Army, married a Chinese nurse and died at thirty-two. China built him memorials, printed his face on stamps and still brings leaders to his family's door. In India, his own country, he is almost unknown.
introduction: Northern China, December 1942. A thirty-two-year-old Indian doctor died there after four years of surgery in a war that was not his own. Within a generation a Chinese city built him a memorial, and India printed his face on a stamp. Yet in the country of his birth his name barely registers. Dwarkanath Shantaram Kotnis was a doctor from a middle-class family in Solapur who answered a call, crossed the sea, and became the rarest thing in either country: a man whom each remembers differently.

chapters.heading: Solapur
paragraphs: Dwarkanath Shantaram Kotnis was born on 10 October 1910 in Sholapur, as Solapur was then spelled, in the Bombay Presidency of British India. He grew up in a middle-class Maharashtrian family. His father, Shantaram Narayan Kotnis, worked in the city's textile mills and held a position in the municipality. Indian government accounts record the family as comfortably established in the town.

Solapur had known plague during his childhood, and the family moved out of the city during one outbreak. He entered medical college intending to become a surgeon. His family hoped he would marry, settle in Solapur and practise near home. He wanted surgery, and he wanted to travel. His sister Manorama remembered that nobody in the family knew much about China in those years; they knew it because men came to the door selling Chinese silk. He asked his family's permission to go, and it was granted.

He studied medicine in Bombay. He entered Seth G. S. Medical College, founded in 1926 by Indian nationalists as an answer to the British-run Grant Medical College, and was caught in a student strike there. He was told to leave and continue his studies at Grant. In 2011 researchers found his old career card at Grant Medical College, recording internships in vaccination and in winter and summer infections — the practical work that would serve him in China. He qualified as a doctor in 1936 with an MBBS and wanted a career in surgery.

The young doctor had a taste for travel that his family did not share, and a determination to work where he was needed. He asked permission before accepting the China posting, and his family agreed. When the call came, he was twenty-seven and unmarried. The decision he made that year took him to the other side of the world. He never saw Solapur again.

media.alt: A black-and-white portrait of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis photographed in China in the 1940s
media.caption: Kotnis in China in the 1940s, in a photograph preserved in Chinese archives and now held on Wikimedia Commons under a public-domain licence.

chapters.heading: The call
paragraphs: In 1937 Japan invaded China, and the war that followed killed millions. China's Nationalists and Communists had formed a united front against the invader, and the Communists' fighting arm was called the Eighth Route Army. The Chinese commander Zhu De wrote to Jawaharlal Nehru asking for doctors. Nehru took the request to the Indian National Congress, which created a committee to raise money and choose a team.

Subhas Chandra Bose, as Congress president, issued a press statement on 30 June 1938. He declared an All-India China Day on 12 June, fixed fund-raising days for 7 to 9 July, and said an ambulance had been ordered from Ford's to be sent straight to Hong Kong. The Congress's fifty-second session passed the resolution. More than seven hundred people answered the call, among them about a hundred doctors. The committee picked five: Madan Mohan Lal Atal of Allahabad, a veteran of medical aid in the Spanish Civil War, who led the team; M. R. Cholkar of Nagpur; Bejoy Kumar Basu and Debesh Mukherjee of Calcutta; and Kotnis from Sholapur. A doctor named Ranen Sen was selected first but refused permission by the British because he was a communist, and he suggested Basu in his place.

On 31 August 1938 a public meeting at Jinnah Hall in Bombay said goodbye to the five. Sarojini Naidu, the poet and independence leader who chaired it, fastened Red Cross bands on their arms and warned them that some, or one of them, might not come back. The next morning they sailed from Ballard Pier on the SS Rajputana. Basu's diary remembers Kotnis so heavily garlanded that nothing showed except his weary, exultant face. The ship called at Colombo, Penang, Singapore and Hong Kong. The party reached Chinese soil at Guangzhou on 17 September. At a banquet there, Basu recorded, Soong Ching-ling, the widow of Sun Yat-sen, watched the Indian doctors struggle with their chopsticks, dipped her hand into the chicken and said: 'God has given fingers to pick up food.' They moved on through Changsha and Hankou, worked with the Chinese Red Cross, went west to Yichang and Chongqing, and reached Yan'an on 12 February 1939.

chapters.heading: Yan'an
paragraphs: Yan'an, in the northern province of Shaanxi, was the wartime capital of the Chinese Communists: a cave-city of party offices, schools and hospitals from which the Eighth Route Army directed the war behind Japanese lines. To an Indian doctor who had known only silk merchants, it was another planet. Kotnis arrived in February 1939 and met Mao Zedong the following month. In July he treated Zhou Enlai, later China's premier, after a fall from a horse. He acquired a Chinese name, Ke Dihua, a phonetic rendering of Kotnis. It is the name carved on the memorials and written in the hospital registers; the English one is the name on the Indian stamp.

In November 1939 he left Yan'an for Wuxiang, headquarters of the Eighth Route Army, and then for the border region the Chinese call Jin-Cha-Ji, where the provinces of Shanxi, Chahar and Hebei meet. This was guerrilla country: villages, mountain tracks and field hospitals that moved when the army moved. Surgery there meant wounds, infection and amputations done with whatever equipment could be carried. Kotnis also taught, and he began writing surgical textbooks for Chinese students who had almost nothing to learn from.

Of the five who had sailed together, some went home. Cholkar returned in May 1939; Mukherjee left the same year after falling ill. Nehru wrote in April 1939 that the mission was likely to remain in China for at least another year, and that Atal and Basu had offered to stay as long as the Chinese wanted them. Kotnis was not named in that appeal, but he stayed the longest. He was one of very few foreigners inside the Communist base area, and movement in and out of it was slow and dangerous once the war settled into its long middle years. The mission had been planned as a year's service. It became the rest of his life.

chapters.heading: The hospital in the mountains
paragraphs: Norman Bethune, a Canadian surgeon, had come to China in 1938 and established medical services for the Communist forces, training doctors and nurses in the base areas. He died of blood poisoning contracted during an operation on 12 November 1939. Kotnis laid a wreath at his tomb and was cast as his successor. In 1941 Kotnis became director of the Bethune International Peace Hospital in Shijiazhuang, in Hebei province. He taught at the Bethune Hygiene School of the Jin-Cha-Ji Military Command and worked on surgical manuals. The hospital and the school carry the Canadian's name; the Indian doctor inherited both.

The Eighth Route Army fought behind Japanese lines, and its medical units moved with the troops. In the Jin-Cha-Ji border region Kotnis was a surgeon and a teacher. He operated on wounds and infections in field hospitals that moved with the army, taught nurses and doctors in a language he had to learn, and compiled surgical manuals in Chinese so that the students he trained could learn from them after he was gone. He worked in a hospital that bore the name of a surgeon who had died two years before he arrived in the region. The Bethune Hygiene School trained medical workers for the Eighth Route Army, and Kotnis taught there while running the hospital.

A letter he wrote in April 1942 survives in a collection of more than seventy of his letters. It was addressed to Bejoy Kumar Basu, the doctor from Calcutta who had sailed with him on the Rajputana and had chosen to remain in China. In it Kotnis tells his friend that he regards 1941 as one of the most important years of his life. He did not explain the reason in that passage. His work continued until his health failed in December of that year.

media.caption: Kotnis laying a wreath in memory of Norman Bethune, the Canadian surgeon whose work with the Eighth Route Army he continued. In 1941 he became director of the hospital that bears Bethune's name.

chapters.heading: Yinhua
paragraphs: In 1941, at the Bethune International Peace Hospital in Shijiazhuang, Kotnis married Guo Qinglan, a Chinese nurse who worked there. The hospital had been named for a Canadian surgeon who died in 1939, so the wedding took place inside a building that was already a memorial to another foreign doctor. She had been working as a nurse at the hospital when they met. In later life she was known as Guo Qinglan Kotnis. Chinese leaders visiting India would ask after her.

Their son was born on 23 August 1942. At the suggestion of Nie Rongzhen, a senior Communist commander, they named him Yinhua. The first character, yin, is the short form of Yin-du, India; the second, hua, is China. Chinese-language records give the boy's full name as Ke Yinhua, using the surname his father had taken. The name was a small act of double belonging, given in a wartime hospital in northern China to a child whose father would not live to see him grow up. The boy was born in the hospital where his father worked, in the middle of the war. It is the most precise thing anyone ever said about this life, and it needs no speech to explain it.

Their son died in 1967, twenty-five years after his father. Guo Qinglan outlived her husband by sixty-nine years. She died in Dalian in 2011 at the age of ninety-six. She had remarried but kept the name Guo Qinglan Kotnis, and for the rest of her life she appeared in the records of her own country as the widow of an Indian doctor who had died in a war between China and Japan.

chapters.heading: The last page
paragraphs: Kotnis had epilepsy. The strain of his work made it worse. He died on 9 December 1942, aged thirty-two, in northern China. His remains were laid in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang, among the martyrs of the wars China fought in the twentieth century. He was one of the few foreigners buried there. His Chinese wife and his infant son were in the country he had made his home.

Chinese state media record that he collapsed on 8 December while writing a second surgery textbook for his Chinese students. He died the following day. The surgeon who had spent four years teaching others was still writing the book he meant them to use when his health gave way.

A 1946 Indian film, Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani, told a dramatised version of his life. It was directed by V. Shantaram and written by K. A. Abbas and V. P. Sathe from Abbas's account And One Did Not Come Back. The real story is plainer and needs no such colour. He was a young doctor chosen by a committee from more than seven hundred volunteers, sent off at a public meeting in Bombay, who worked in field hospitals until his body failed. Nehru, who had received Zhu De's appeal, appealed in April 1939 for funds to keep the mission in China. Kotnis stayed when the others went home. He left behind a Chinese wife, a son not yet four months old, and a memory that survived in a land he had once known only through silk sellers.

media.alt: The tomb of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang, Hebei province
media.caption: His Chinese-style tomb in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery at Shijiazhuang. His remains were brought here after his death in 1942.

chapters.heading: A hero in two countries
paragraphs: V. Shantaram's 1946 film Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani, written by K. A. Abbas and V. P. Sathe from Abbas's piece And One Did Not Come Back, made Kotnis a household name in India for a time. China made its own film, Ke Di Hua Dai Fu, in 1982. China issued stamps bearing his face in 1982 and 1992; India followed with a commemorative stamp on 9 December 1993. In 2009 a Chinese internet poll named him among the ten foreign friends who had done most for China in a century. Chinese leaders have called on his family in India for decades, a ritual of a friendship that predates the border war of 1962.

There is a memorial to him in Shijiazhuang and a memorial hall in Tang County, where he worked and died. A hall at the Bethune International Peace Hospital carries his name, as does the Kotnis India-China Friendship Hospital at Hebei Medical University. In Solapur, a memorial hospital opened in 1976 and his former residence became a memorial in 2012. New exhibition halls opened in Hebei in December 2025. Official Chinese media call him Dr Thoughtful and Old Ke. The Indian historian Vinay Lal wrote of adulation, even veneration, in China, and of Kotnis being largely forgotten in India.

The BBC wrote in 2013 that at home Dr Kotnis appears to be a little-known figure, while in China he is revered as a hero. The generation that saw the 1946 film has passed, and the other four doctors of the mission have faded from memory too. The 1962 war between India and China changed how each country told the story. What remains is a name on a hospital in Hebei, a name on a street in Solapur, a stamp in an album, and a son's two-character name that joins the two countries more neatly than any treaty.

media.alt: A memorial statue of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis at the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang
media.caption: The memorial statue at Shijiazhuang, where his remains were laid in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery after his death in 1942.

chapters.heading: What remains
paragraphs: A young Indian doctor with a taste for travel and surgery took a ship to a country he knew through silk salesmen. He learned its language, worked in hospitals that moved with an army, taught its students from books he wrote himself, married one of its nurses and gave his son a name made of both countries. He died at thirty-two and was buried among China's martyrs. India printed his face on a stamp in 1993. He had sailed from Bombay in September 1938 at the age of twenty-seven and never returned. China kept his memory because he served its people during the war against Japan. India let it go.

The record survives in ordinary things: Nehru's appeal for the mission, Basu's diary of the voyage, the career card found at Grant Medical College, more than seventy letters preserved in a Chinese collection, two countries' postage stamps, a film catalogue entry, and a grave in Shijiazhuang. The Indian historian Vinay Lal described the result in one sentence: adulation, even veneration, in China; largely forgotten in India.

The photograph on this page came back from China. That is where his memory survived, and that is where a reader has to go to find him. In Solapur, the town of his birth, a memorial hospital opened in 1976 and his former residence became a memorial in 2012. In Hebei, where he spent the last years of his life, a memorial hall stands in Tang County and new exhibition halls opened in December 2025. China issued its own stamps in 1982 and 1992; India issued one in 1993. The two films, Indian in 1946 and Chinese in 1982, remain the screen records of his life. Two countries, one doctor, and a name that neither has quite let go.

media.alt: The 1993 Indian postage stamp commemorating Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis, showing his portrait
media.caption: India Post issued this stamp on 9 December 1993, fifty-one years after his death. It is the clearest sign that the country which sent him had begun to remember him too.
media.credit: India Post, Government of India — GODL-India

sources.note: By surgeon-historian Sanjay Nagral. Supports the plague outbreak that led the family to leave Solapur, his admission to Seth G. S. Medical College and his move to Grant after a student strike, his 1936 qualification, and his family's wish that he settle in Solapur.

sources.title: 'Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis' feature and biography

sources.note: Indian government account. Supports the 10 October 1910 birth, the middle-class family, the five mission doctors, his wish to travel and practise surgery, his family's permission, his sister Manorama's recollection, the 1946 film and the 1993 Indian stamp.

sources.title: 'Why is India's Dr Kotnis revered in China?'
sources.note: Supports the marriage to Guo Qinglan, the 2009 Chinese internet poll, Chinese leaders visiting his family, and the contrast between his status in China and his obscurity in India.

sources.note: Academic account by Vinay Lal. Supports the reading of Kotnis as a figure of pre-1962 India-China solidarity and the contrast between veneration in China and being forgotten in India.

sources.title: 'The undying influence and memory of Dr Kotnis'
sources.note: Indian think-tank reconstruction. Supports the itinerary — Yan'an in February 1939, the meeting with Mao in March, treating Zhou Enlai in July, Wuxiang and Jin-Cha-Ji — and the naming of his son Yinhua.
